samples.summary: READ_GATED_METHODS lets a viewer-role share token write: the AttachDocument change pack is applied under a read-only decision
samples.evidence:
Pre-change, `checkAttribute` computed `needWrite = attr.verb === 'rw' || REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method)`, so an `AttachDocument` (which Yorkie always sends with verb `rw`, per packages/backend/test/revision-history.e2e-spec.ts:373) required write authority. The new line 286 (`attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method)`) drops that: attach is now authorized with `needWrite=false`, and `hasAccess` returns true for ANY viewer share link bound to that document (line 322: `return needWrite ? link.role === 'editor' : true`).

Full vector, all with public inputs: (1) an anonymous visitor loads a public template card and receives `previewToken` (template.service.ts:1314), which is a share link created with role `'viewer'` (template.service.ts:374); (2) POSTs it to the unauthenticated `POST /auth/yorkie-token/share` (auth.controller.ts:82) and gets a signed `{typ:'yorkie-share'}` token; (3) builds a bare `yorkie.Client` with the project public key that ships in every visitor's bundle, calls `doc.update(...)` on a local Document BEFORE `client.attach(doc)` so the mutation rides the attach ChangePack; (4) the webhook sees method `AttachDocument`, skips the write check, returns ALLOW, and the Yorkie server applies the pack. Detach + re-attach repeats it without limit.

So, even with `YORKIE_AUTH_WEBHOOK_ENFORCE` enforcing and every method registered, a read-only share link (and the gallery's preview token) is write-capable. That is precisely the consequence `assertYorkieAuthEnforced` (template-review.ts:104) gates the public tier on preventing — and the gate now attests something it no longer buys, since one attach per card is as cheap as the one request per card the gate's own comment describes. The change documents this as a "residual", but the weakening is introduced here in the same change that makes enforcement the default and re-opens the public tier on the strength of it; the accompanying claim that only a "non-browser client" can do it is not a security boundary (the attacker writes the client).

samples.summary: The `yorkie-service` token is an unscoped all-document read/write credential, and the rationale that it "never leaves the process" is false — it is transmitted to every Yorkie server the backend and the ops scripts talk to
samples.evidence:
`decide()` returns ALLOW for `identity.typ === 'yorkie-service'` before any document key, verb, attribute-presence or revision-method check runs, so one token authorizes read, write, `RestoreRevision`, and every other gated RPC on every document key in the deployment for its full 10-minute lifetime.

The security argument for that blast radius is stated in packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-service-token.ts:24 — "it never leaves the process, so nothing but a secret compromise can produce one". That premise is wrong by construction: the token is exactly what `authTokenInjector` hands the Yorkie SDK, so it is sent over the wire to `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` on every RPC (yorkie.service.ts:73), and copy-yorkie-documents.ts:258-262 deliberately sends one to a *different deployment's* Yorkie server. `YORKIE_RPC_ADDR` defaults to plain `http://` (yorkie.service.ts:31) and nothing forbids an http address across a network, so the credential can also travel in cleartext. Anywhere the Yorkie server or a proxy in front of it records request headers, that log now contains an all-documents read/write credential rather than a single user's.

The webhook body carries the document key it is deciding, so the token could have been minted bound to that key (`{typ:'yorkie-service', docKey}`) and compared in `checkAttribute`, bounding a leak to the document the server-side attach actually needed. As written there is no scoping of any kind. Confidence is medium because replaying the token at the webhook additionally requires a valid `YORKIE_SECRET_KEY` HMAC (yorkie-signature.guard.ts), so the practical holder is the Yorkie deployment and its logs rather than an arbitrary network attacker.

samples.summary: The ops scripts require the deployments' raw `JWT_SECRET` (the session-signing key) in an operator/CI shell, so running a document copy now needs a secret that forges any user's session
samples.evidence:
`sideTokenInjector` reads `SOURCE_JWT_SECRET` / `TARGET_JWT_SECRET` and the usage text (line 69-75) tells the operator to set them to "the <side> deployment's own JWT_SECRET"; `yorkieServiceTokenInjectorFromEnv` (yorkie-service-token.ts:76) defaults to `process.env.JWT_SECRET` for the two migrate scripts. `JWT_SECRET` is `AuthService.accessSecret` (auth.service.ts:58) — the key the *session access token* is signed with, and the key `JwtStrategy` verifies bearer sessions against (jwt.strategy.ts:24). Anyone who can read that environment (a CI secret store, `ps e` / `/proc/<pid>/environ` on the operator box, a shell dump, an accidental `env` in a job log) can sign `{sub: <any user id>, tokenType:'access'}` and authenticate as any user of that deployment — and, when `JWT_REFRESH_SECRET` is unset, mint refresh tokens too (auth.service.ts:60).

The change already reasons carefully about argv vs environment, but the residual risk is the *kind* of secret being distributed, not its channel: the script only needs a short-lived `{typ:'yorkie-service'}` JWT, which the deployment could mint and hand over (e.g. `SOURCE_YORKIE_SERVICE_TOKEN`), so the signing key never has to leave the server. As written, a cross-deployment copy escalates from "operator holds two database URLs" to "operator holds two full impersonation keys".

samples.summary: The script's own new rule against secrets on argv is not applied to `--database-url`, `--mongo-url` or `--source-api-key`
samples.evidence: The added comment at line 31-33 states the rule ("A secret on the command line is readable by any local process through `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and is echoed into shell history and CI logs") and applies it only to the JWT secrets. The same invocation still passes `--database-url` and `--mongo-url` (lines 92-99), which are Postgres/Mongo connection strings containing credentials for the deployment's primary datastores, plus `--source-api-key`, on argv — and the usage block printed at line 59-67 instructs the operator to do exactly that. Either those should move to the environment too, or the new comment should say why they are treated differently; as it stands the stated threat model is documented and then not followed for the higher-value credentials in the same command line.

samples.summary: The new notes share route adds another consumer of an editor share token passed in a URL query string, where it lands in access logs and Referer headers
samples.evidence: `shareTokenImageUploader(token)` (image-insert.ts:40) calls `postShareTokenImage`, which puts the share token in the request URL: `/api/v1/shared/images?token=${encodeURIComponent(token)}` (packages/frontend/src/api/images.ts:57), consumed by `@Query('token')` in image-share-upload.controller.ts:95. An editor-role share token is a bearer credential that grants anonymous write to the document and image uploads into its workspace prefix, and query strings are the one part of a request that reverse proxies, CDNs and application access logs record by default. The repo already reasons about this elsewhere and chose a POST body for the same class of credential ("Uses POST with the share token in the body so the (access-granting) token stays out of request URLs and access logs", auth.controller.ts:78-80). The route/API is pre-existing, so this is a pre-existing weakness, but this change widens its exposure to the notes share surface; a header (or body field) would keep it out of logs.

verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as quoted. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:108 defines READ_GATED_METHODS = {'AttachDocument'}; lines 284-286 compute needWrite = REVISION_READ_METHODS.has(method) ? true : attr.verb === 'rw' && !READ_GATED_METHODS.has(method), so an AttachDocument (which Yorkie sends with verb 'rw') yields needWrite=false; line 322 then returns true for ANY share link bound to the document regardless of role, i.e. a viewer-role link is authorized on attach. The attack chain is reachable with public inputs: POST /auth/yorkie-token/share (auth.controller.ts:82-90) has no JwtAuthGuard and mints a Yorkie token from any share token; template.service.ts:372-375 creates the template preview link with role 'viewer' and template.service.ts:1314 exposes it as previewToken on publicly visible listings (isVisibleTo, 1186-1199); DetachDocument is unconditionally allowed (yorkie-auth.controller.ts:221-223), enabling unlimited detach/re-attach. No guard elsewhere blocks a viewer's attach change pack — the repository's own docs affirm the opposite (template-review.ts:88-100: 'a client that puts its change pack in the attach itself gets that pack applied, and re-attaching repeats it'; README.md:226; docs/design/yorkie-auth-webhook.md:285). A documented/accepted residual is still a real authorization weakness, and 'requires a non-browser client' is not a security boundary. This is authorization/access-control, squarely in the Security lane, with critical impact (anonymous write to any publicly previewable template document).

verdict.reason: Code is present exactly as described. yorkie-auth.controller.ts:240-242 returns ALLOW for identity.typ === YORKIE_SERVICE_TOKEN_TYPE before the empty-attribute fail-closed check (line 253) and before any per-key/verb/method authorization in checkAttribute (lines 261-266, 271-291), so one service token authorizes read, write, GetRevision/ListRevisions and every other gated RPC on every document key for its full lifetime. The safety rationale at yorkie-service-token.ts:23 ("it never leaves the process") is demonstrably false: yorkieServiceTokenInjector (lines 54-62) is the authTokenInjector handed to the Yorkie SDK at yorkie.service.ts:73, with rpcAddr defaulting to plain http:// (lines 40-42); the webhook only sees the token because it travelled to the Yorkie server and back (controller line 227). copy-yorkie-documents.ts:255-263 sends service tokens to two external Yorkie deployments. No guard makes this unreachable: YorkieSignatureGuard only proves the caller is Yorkie, and any client holding the public project key can attach with a leaked service token, causing Yorkie to sign the webhook call itself; verifyYorkieToken performs only signature/expiry checks with no scope claim (auth.service.spec.ts:94-127). One reviewer detail is imprecise — sideTokenInjector (copy-yorkie-documents.ts:40-54) deliberately prevents one deployment's secret from being used against another's server — but that does not touch the load-bearing claim of an unscoped, network-transmitted all-documents credential. In-lane (authorization/credential scoping, sensitive credential exposure) and not refutable on any named ground.

That secret is provably the session key: auth.service.ts:58 sets `accessSecret` from `JWT_SECRET`, :118-124 signs `{tokenType:'access', sub}` with it, jwt.strategy.ts:24 verifies bearer sessions against it, and :59-60 falls back to it for refresh tokens. Holding it therefore permits forging a session for any user. The scripts only require a `{typ:'yorkie-service'}` token (yorkie-service-token.ts:38-46, accepted by auth.service.ts:95-107), so a pre-minted token is a viable lesser credential. No guard constrains the env var (only a console.warn when absent). The 'operator already has DB creds' counterexample fails because the target deployment contributes only `TARGET_JWT_SECRET` and an RPC addr (:260-263) — no target DB URL — so it is a genuine privilege escalation for that side. In-lane under 'secrets / sensitive data exposure', major per the rubric.
